No, I don't think so. I mean, it's not like a blackout or anything like that. I remember standing there. Well, no, not really. I mean, between those weird stuck moments, my brain feels totally normal. I must have stood there doing it for twenty minutes before the bartender walked back and asked if I was okay. So... I guess I'm not really sure if stress has anything to do with it, because it seems to happen whether I'm carrying a tray of hot food through a crowd or just standing in an empty room doing side work. It's just so unpredictable, which honestly is what stresses me out the most now. The not knowing when the record is going to skip again.\n\nDoctor: During these episodes, do you ever feel like you are choosing or acting them out on purpose?\n\nPatient: No, no, definitely not on purpose. I mean, why would I? It's embarrassing. It's so embarrassing. Like with the napkin thing I just mentioned, folding and unfolding it... if I was doing that on purpose, I would have stopped the second I realized how ridiculous it looked. But I couldn't. It's like... it's like my hands were doing it, and my brain was watching my hands do it, but there was no connection between the two. There's no part of me that thinks, \"Oh, I'm going to stand by the soda machine and say table numbers now.\" I don't want to do these things. I want to be working. I need my job. I have rent, I have my car payment—it's a 2014 Civic, and it's mostly reliable, but it needs new brake pads soon, and I can't afford that if I'm not picking up shifts. So, no, I'm not choosing this. It feels like the opposite of choosing. It feels like the choice is completely taken away from me. I'm just sort of trapped inside the action while it's happening, waiting for it to be over, waiting for someone to snap me out of it so I can just go back to being normal and doing my job. I'd give anything to just be able to choose to stop when it happens.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a seizure?\n\nPatient: A seizure? Like, falling down and shaking? No, I've never had anything like that. I mean, my aunt on my mom's side had epilepsy, I think? Or maybe it was my great-aunt. I remember my mom talking about it when I was really little, how they had to be careful with flashing lights and stuff. But I've never had anything like that happen to me. I've never passed out or convulsed or bitten my tongue. And like I was saying before, I'm completely awake when these weird stuck moments happen. My eyes are open, I'm standing up, I'm not falling over or losing my balance. I'm just... frozen in whatever I'm doing. So it doesn't feel like a medical emergency in that way, you know? It's not like my body is spasming. It's just my actions that get stuck. I've never even fainted in my life, honestly. Not even when I had to get my blood drawn for a physical a few years ago, and I hate needles. I get super lightheaded, but I always stay conscious. So, no, definitely no seizures. Unless... I mean, unless there's a type of seizure where you just stand there and repeat things? But even then, I feel like a doctor would have caught that when I was younger. I was a pretty healthy kid, mostly just ear infections and stuff. So, yeah, no seizures that I know of.\n\nDoctor: When these episodes happen, do you find yourself making the same repetitive movements over and over, like folding, tapping, or repeating actions in a fixed pattern?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I mean, like I was saying with the napkin, right? What really scared everyone, and honestly scared me too, is that I started freezing up right in the middle of service. Like, right in the thick of it. I'll be in the middle of doing something completely normal, and then I just... derail. Like, the other day, I was supposed to be closing out checks. We have this old point-of-sale system, it's super clunky, you have to use a physical key to pop the cash drawer if you're settling a cash payment. So I had the cash drawer key in my hand, and I was standing by the soda station, which isn't even where the terminal is. The terminal is on the other side of the server alley. Just standing there going, \"Table 42, table 12, table 42, table 12.\" Over and over. And I wasn't closing the checks. I was just holding the key and saying the numbers. My manager, Dave, he had to physically come over and touch my arm and say my name a few times to get me to stop. It's not just tapping or folding, it's like my whole sequence of actions gets scrambled and then gets stuck on a loop. Like I said about my manager, Dave, when I was doing the table numbers thing? He had to come over and physically touch my arm. And even then, it wasn't like, *boom*, I'm back. It's more like... like waking up from a really deep sleep where you're still groggy and confused for a second. He was saying my name, \"Sarah, Sarah,\" and I heard him, but it felt like he was talking to me from underwater at first. And then I felt his hand on my arm, and that physical contact kind of pulled me back. But if someone just shouts at me from across the room? Like, if a customer was like, \"Hey, waitress, stop doing that!\" I don't know if that would work. It really seems to take someone getting right in my space, breaking that loop physically or repeating my name a few times until it finally registers. So, yeah, I can stop, eventually, but it takes a lot of effort from whoever is trying to help me, and it's never just a simple \"hey, cut it out\" kind of thing. It's a whole process to get me un-stuck.\n\nDoctor: Between these episodes, have you noticed any changes in your memory, attention, or ability to think clearly in everyday life?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not really. I have rent, I have my car payment—it's a 2014 Civic, and it's mostly reliable, but it needs new brake pads soon, and I can't afford that if I'm not picking up shifts. So, no, I'm not choosing this. It feels like the opposite of choosing. It feels like the choice is completely taken away from me. I'm just sort of trapped inside the action while it's happening, waiting for it to be over, waiting for someone to snap me out of it so I can just go back to being normal and doing my job. I'd give anything to just be able to choose to stop when it happens.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a seizure?\n\nPatient: A seizure? Like, falling down and shaking? No, I've never had anything like that. I mean, my aunt on my mom's side had epilepsy, I think? Or maybe it was my great-aunt. I remember my mom talking about it when I was really little, how they had to be careful with flashing lights and stuff. But I've never had anything like that happen to me. I've never passed out or convulsed or bitten my tongue. And like I was saying before, I'm completely awake when these weird stuck moments happen. My eyes are open, I'm standing up, I'm not falling over or losing my balance. I'm just... frozen in whatever I'm doing. So it doesn't feel like a medical emergency in that way, you know? It's not like my body is spasming. It's just my actions that get stuck. I've never even fainted in my life, honestly. Not even when I had to get my blood drawn for a physical a few years ago, and I hate needles. I get super lightheaded, but I always stay conscious. So, no, definitely no seizures. Unless... I mean, unless there's a type of seizure where you just stand there and repeat things? But even then, I feel like a doctor would have caught that when I was younger. I was a pretty healthy kid, mostly just ear infections and stuff. So, yeah, no seizures that I know of.\n\nDoctor: When these episodes happen, do you find yourself making the same repetitive movements over and over, like folding, tapping, or repeating actions in a fixed pattern?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I mean, like I was saying with the napkin, right? What really scared everyone, and honestly scared me too, is that I started freezing up right in the middle of service. Like, right in the thick of it. I'll be in the middle of doing something completely normal, and then I just... derail. Like, the other day, I was supposed to be closing out checks. We have this old point-of-sale system, it's super clunky, you have to use a physical key to pop the cash drawer if you're settling a cash payment.
